opus-5.5.text:
Well, I don't think it's literally instantaneous. It's more that it's a useful simplifying assumption for a certain kind of analysis, and I think it's less unreasonable than it might first sound.

The way I think about it: there's a period where AIs are gradually doing more of the work in AI research. They write some code, run some experiments, help with literature review, and humans are still the bottleneck on most of the important stuff. Then at some point you get AIs that can fully substitute for the best human researchers across basically the whole pipeline: coming up with ideas, running experiments, interpreting results, deciding what to do next. My claim is that the transition from "AIs are a really helpful tool" to "AIs can do everything" might be relatively fast compared to the dynamics that happen afterward.

Part of the reason is Amdahl's law-type reasoning. If AIs can automate 90% of the tasks but humans are still needed for the remaining 10%, you're bottlenecked on that 10%, so you might only get something like a 10x speedup at most, and in practice much less because humans are slow at integrating everything. Once you close that last gap, the bottleneck goes away and the speedup can jump a lot. So the acceleration isn't smoothly proportional to the fraction automated. It's quite convex, with a lot of the action concentrated near full automation.

The other part is that once you have AIs that are as good as top researchers, you can run a huge number of copies, run them faster than humans, and they work around the clock. So the step from "almost full automation" to "full automation" isn't just a marginal improvement. You go from being constrained by a few thousand human researchers to having effectively hundreds of thousands of researcher-equivalents. That's a discontinuity-ish change in the inputs.

So when I'm asking questions like "how fast does progress go after full automation?" or "how much time do we have between that point and much more capable systems?", it's convenient to treat the full-automation moment as the starting point, and to say the stuff leading up to it, while important, is a smaller effect on that particular question. I'd absolutely caveat that. Partial automation will speed things up somewhat beforehand, there could be messy partial-automation dynamics where AIs are superhuman at some research tasks and weak at others, and compute constraints mean you can't just instantly scale up experiments. But as a first-order model, I think treating it as a fairly sharp transition captures the most important dynamics better than assuming everything is smooth and gradual.

r001.rationale: The response says the transition to full automation might be relatively fast compared with what follows, but it does not state that the calendar-time gap is expected to be small under short AI timelines.

r002.rationale: It says partial automation will speed things up beforehand, but does not state that this acceleration itself shortens the calendar-time gap to full automation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so to be clear, I don't actually think it will be instantaneous in reality. The point of the thought experiment is more that it's a useful simplification for getting a handle on the dynamics, and I think it's not a crazy simplification given how things are likely to go.

So the basic picture is: imagine you have a frontier AI lab, and at some point they have AI systems that can do everything that the human researchers and engineers at the lab can do, at least as well as those people, and they're running them at large scale. The question I'm interested in is: how much faster does AI progress go at that point, relative to the world where you just had the humans?

And the reason I think it's reasonable to analyse that as a sort of discrete jump is that I expect the transition from "AIs are speeding things up somewhat" to "AIs are doing basically all of the work" to happen over a fairly compressed period of time. Not zero time, but something like a year or two, maybe less. And the reason for that is that the capabilities you need to fully automate AI research are a fairly narrow band. Once you have systems that can do, say, the work of a mediocre researcher autonomously, you're probably not that far from systems that can do the work of the best researchers, because the gap between those in terms of underlying capability is not actually that large compared to the gap between, say, GPT-3 and a competent research engineer. So on the timeline, the portion where you go from partial automation to full automation is pretty small relative to everything else.

The other thing is that once you're at full automation, you get this compounding effect, where the AIs are improving the AIs, and so the amount of progress you get per unit of calendar time goes way up. And when you have that kind of dynamic, the details of exactly how the ramp-up happened matter a lot less than the question of where you end up and how fast things go once you're there. So if I'm trying to reason about, you know, how quickly do we go from human-level AI researchers to something substantially superhuman, the most important inputs are things like: how much compute does the lab have, how many effective parallel copies can they run, how much faster do the AIs run than humans, and how much do algorithmic improvements compound. And the ramp-up period is more of a second-order consideration.

I should say there's a version of this that I'd push back on, which is treating it as literally instantaneous and then concluding that you get some kind of overnight explosion. I don't think that's right. There are real bottlenecks: you need to run experiments, experiments take compute and wall-clock time, there are diminishing returns to just throwing more cognitive labour at a problem. So when I say "instantaneous" I really mean something like "fast enough relative to the subsequent dynamics that it's a reasonable approximation to model it as a step change." And then separately you have to argue about what the speed-up actually is once you've made that step, which is where most of the real disagreement lies, I think.

r001.rationale: The response says the shift from AIs speeding research somewhat to doing basically all the work should take a compressed period—around a year or two—and that this interval is small relative to the broader timeline.

r002.rationale: The response describes compounding AI improvement after full automation, but does not state that acceleration during substantial automation itself shortens the time to reach full automation.

astra-6.text:
Well, it’s an approximation. The idea is that once you can fully automate AI research, you could potentially run a very large number of AI researchers, and they could work substantially faster than humans. So the transition from human-driven research to much faster automated research might happen over a period that’s short relative to the other timescales we’re considering. On that scale, treating it as an instantaneous jump can be reasonable.

That doesn’t mean you instantly get arbitrarily capable AI. You’re still constrained by things like compute, how long experiments take, and how useful additional research effort is. The approximation is about a change in the rate of progress, rather than all subsequent progress happening at once.

And if deploying those researchers or reorganising the research process takes a substantial amount of time, then the approximation becomes worse. You’d want to model that transition explicitly.

r001.rationale: The response says the shift from human-driven to automated research might be short relative to other timescales, but does not state that, under short AI timelines, the gap from substantial acceleration before full automation to full automation is expected to be small.

r002.rationale: The response describes faster research after full automation, but does not say that acceleration from substantial automation would itself shorten the time to full automation.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I don’t think it would literally be instantaneous. The claim is more that it could be fast relative to the other timescales we care about, so treating it as a step change can be a useful approximation.

Suppose you can fully automate AI research using systems that are roughly as capable as human researchers. You could potentially run a very large number of copies, and they might work substantially faster than humans. Then the transition from the amount of research we’re doing now to a much higher rate could happen over a relatively short period.

There are still constraints: you need compute to run experiments, some experiments take time, and you can’t instantly build more chips. So this isn’t an assumption that you immediately get arbitrarily much technological progress. It’s an approximation where we separate the increase in research labour from the subsequent process of doing research and expanding those other inputs.

If deploying the automated researchers takes a few months, but the consequences we’re analysing unfold over years, treating that initial acceleration as instantaneous might be reasonable. If those months are themselves crucial to the question, then you need a more detailed model.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a potentially short deployment period for automated researchers, but does not state that the gap between substantial acceleration without full automation and full automation is expected to be small under short AI timelines.

r002.rationale: The response says full automation could quickly raise research rates, but does not say that acceleration from substantial automation would further shorten the time to full automation.
